batchName: Middle Republic: Scipio and the Road to Zama (216-201 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Middle Republic: Scipio and the Road to Zama (216-201 BCE)

questions.question: In what year did Rome finally destroy the city of Carthage?
questions.explanation: After the peace of 201 BC Carthage was plainly subordinate to Rome, and Rome destroyed the city altogether in 146 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Carthage was now plainly subordinate to Rome, and in 146 BC Rome destroyed the city altogether.

questions.question: About how old was Scipio when he received the Spanish command in 210 BC?
questions.explanation: The people's assembly gave the Spanish command to Scipio when he was about 25. Normally only a man who had held a senior office could lead an army in his own right.
questions.sourceQuote: In 210 BC the people's assembly gave the Spanish command to the younger Scipio, then about 25.

questions.question: Beside which river was the army of Hannibal's brother trapped and destroyed in 207 BC?
questions.explanation: After a night retreat, the Carthaginian army was trapped beside the Metaurus in north-east Italy. Hannibal's brother died in the battle that followed.
questions.sourceQuote: His guides deserted him, and dawn found his weary army trapped beside the Metaurus, a river in north-east Italy.

questions.question: At which battle in 206 BC did Scipio deliver the decisive blow against the Carthaginians in Spain?
questions.explanation: At Ilipa, north of modern Seville, Scipio routed the remaining Carthaginian forces and drove them from the peninsula.
questions.sourceQuote: The decisive blow fell in 206 BC at Ilipa, north of modern Seville.

questions.question: How did Scipio destroy the two enemy armies camped near Utica in 203 BC?
options: He starved them out with a long blockade
He flooded their camps by diverting a river
He set their camps ablaze in a night attack
He drove war elephants through their lines
questions.explanation: Scipio split his army one evening and set the Numidian camp on fire. In the chaos his men also fell on the Carthaginian camp, and thousands died in the dark.
questions.sourceQuote: One evening in 203 BC he marched out, split his army, and set the Numidian camp ablaze.

questions.question: What happened to Scipio's father and uncle in Spain in 211 BC?
options: They were taken prisoner and later ransomed
They captured New Carthage and were celebrated
They split their forces, were beaten separately and killed
They were recalled to Rome in disgrace
questions.explanation: The brothers divided their forces to attack three enemy armies at once, and each was defeated and killed. Two of the victorious Carthaginian commanders were Hannibal's own brothers.
questions.sourceQuote: Each was beaten separately, and both men were killed.

questions.question: In which arm did Scipio outnumber Hannibal at Zama, despite having fewer men overall?
questions.explanation: Scipio had more than 6,000 cavalry, many brought by Masinissa, against only 4,000 on Hannibal's side. Hannibal still had more men overall, about 40,000.
questions.sourceQuote: Scipio had around 29,000 to 30,000 men but more than 6,000 cavalry, many of them brought by Masinissa, the Numidian king allied to Rome.

questions.question: Which Numidian prince, who had once fought for Carthage in Spain, became Rome's most valuable ally?
questions.explanation: Masinissa joined Rome after his rival drove him from his kingdom. He became Rome's most valuable ally.
questions.sourceQuote: When his rival drove him from his kingdom, Masinissa joined Rome and became its most valuable ally.

questions.question: Which god did Scipio tell his troops had promised him help in a vision at New Carthage?
questions.explanation: Scipio claimed the sea god Neptune had promised him help. The story fed a growing legend that Scipio was a favourite of the gods.
questions.sourceQuote: He told his troops that the sea god Neptune had promised him help in a vision.

questions.question: Later versions of the Scipio legend made him the son of which god?
questions.explanation: Later legend made Scipio a son of Jupiter, Rome's chief god. Even in his lifetime, tales spread of divine visions and prophetic dreams.
questions.sourceQuote: Later versions even made him a son of Jupiter, Rome's chief god.
